subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: asking the police or shop counter to display a notice [Action]
passage: Rain drummed on the tin roof of the Shivpur bus stand when Yogesh spotted a cloth bag wedged under the bench. Inside were bundles of notes held with rubber bands. His school bus was due in ten minutes. Yogesh looked around; nobody seemed to be searching. He closed the bag and carried it to the tea stall. "Bhaiya, someone lost this. Can you call the police?" The stall owner, Sachin, wiped his hands and dialled the chowki. Yogesh waited, one eye on the road, until a constable arrived on a scooter, counted the bundles in front of them both and wrote Yogesh's name in a register. "The owner will have to tell us the colour of the bag and what is inside," the constable said. Yogesh ran for his bus, soaked but light on his feet.

qa.q: What was inside the cloth bag?
qa.a: Bundles of notes held with rubber bands.

qa.q: What might Yogesh have been worried about while he waited at the stall?
qa.a: He was anxious about missing his school bus, yet he kept waiting because he wanted the money to reach safe hands first.

qa.q: What else could Yogesh have done if the tea stall had been closed?
qa.a: He could have taken the bag to the ticket counter or a bus conductor at the stand, since a known adult in a fixed place can pass it to the police.

qa.q: How does this plan look to the person who lost the bag?
qa.a: They can get it back only by describing the bag and what is inside, so nobody can simply walk up and claim it.

grounding: A child who finds cash at a bus stand gets a nearby stall owner to call the police, who keep it until the owner can describe it.

subtopic: Found money or a lost wallet
subtype: Approach: asking the police or shop counter to display a notice [Action]
passage: Lunchtime at the Karol Nagar bus stop. Tenzin was waiting for his aunt when he noticed a zipped pouch lying beside the bench leg. He opened it just enough to see a thick fold of notes and a bus pass with no name. His heart thumped. Chetan-uncle, who ran the tea stall across the footpath, was pouring glasses for two drivers. Tenzin walked over and held out the pouch. "I found this. Will you ring the police chowki? I don't want to keep it." Chetan-uncle made the call, and a constable came and took the pouch away. Twenty minutes later, while Tenzin was still at the stop, a woman hurried back, searching under the bench. Tenzin pointed her to the stall. At the chowki she described the pouch and the pass, and got it back.

qa.q: Who ran the tea stall across the footpath?
qa.a: Chetan-uncle ran the tea stall.

qa.q: What does Tenzin's thumping heart suggest?
qa.a: He felt nervous and uneasy holding so much money that was not his, which is why he did not want to keep it.

qa.q: Which approach would suit Tenzin if the stall had been empty?
qa.a: He could wait for his aunt and ask her to take the pouch to the chowki with him, because a child should hand found money to a trusted adult rather than carry it around.

qa.q: What is it like for the woman when she finds the bench empty?
qa.a: She is probably panicked at first, then relieved when Tenzin points her to the stall and she gets the pouch back by describing it.

grounding: The passage shows a child asking a tea-stall owner to phone the police so the rightful owner can later identify and claim the money.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
passage: Jasleen, you keep asking why this old tea tin has three lids. Sit. When I was ten, my mother began giving me two hundred rupees on the first of each month. The first month I spent all of it on sweets by the fifth day, then cried when the bookshop got the bird book I wanted. So I sat on the back step and argued with myself. "If I buy nothing, I'm miserable. If I buy everything, I'm miserable later." I found three tins. One for treats now, one for the bird book, and one small one for giving: the temple box, or my friend Dawa, whose father was out of work. Every month I, Pema, thought again about how much went where. That is why the lids are three.

qa.q: How much money did Pema's mother give on the first of each month?
qa.a: Two hundred rupees.

qa.q: What was Pema feeling while arguing on the back step?
qa.a: Pema felt torn: buying nothing seemed miserable, but spending everything had already left Pema miserable when the bird book came.

qa.q: Which choice inside the story made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Setting up three separate tins, because it turned one big temptation each month into a small, visible split that could be rethought every month.

qa.q: How might Dawa have been affected by the giving tin?
qa.a: Dawa, whose father was out of work, may have felt cared for, though perhaps a little awkward about receiving help from a friend.

grounding: An elder recalls dividing monthly pocket money into tins for treats, saving and giving, reasoning it through as a child.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: splitting money into spend, save and give [Thinking]
passage: The two hundred rupees came late this month, on the fifteenth, and the school fair was only two days away. Madhuri spread the notes on her bed while her little brother Vijay watched. "If I take it all to the fair, the storybook I'm saving for moves further away," she said aloud. "But if I take nothing, I'll just stand there watching everyone eat." She folded a hundred into the jar marked FAIR. Seventy went into the jar with the book's picture taped on it. She held the last thirty for a long moment. "Class is collecting for Ritesh's family after the flood," she told Vijay. "Thirty is small, but it's something." Vijay nodded seriously and dropped his own five-rupee coin into that jar.

qa.q: When did the money come this month?
qa.a: On the fifteenth, only two days before the school fair.

qa.q: How can you tell Madhuri felt unsure about the last thirty rupees?
qa.a: She held it for a long moment, showing she felt torn between keeping it and giving it, before deciding that a small amount still helps.

qa.q: What else could Madhuri do if the fair jar feels too tight this month?
qa.a: She could talk it over with a parent and move a little between jars just this once, since the split is her own plan to adjust, not a fixed rule.

qa.q: How does Vijay seem to see his sister's plan?
qa.a: He watches seriously and adds his own coin, so the giving jar seems to inspire him to join in. 🙂

grounding: A girl thinks aloud as she splits her late monthly money into jars for the fair, a book and a class collection.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: saving for a specific goal [Action]
passage: The football in the sports shop at the Sector 9 market cost four hundred rupees. Jatin got fifty every Monday. At home he took a pencil: "Fifty, a hundred, one-fifty..." He counted on until he reached four hundred. Eight Mondays. He drew eight squares on a sheet and taped it inside his cupboard door. His cousin, Minakshi-didi, gave him an old tiffin box to keep the notes in. The hard part was break time, when the canteen smelled of masala chips. In week three he bought one packet and had to leave a square half-coloured, which meant one extra week. After that he carried peanuts from home. On the ninth Monday he walked to the market with the tiffin box and came back bouncing the ball down the stairs.

qa.q: How many squares did Jatin draw on the sheet?
qa.a: Eight squares.

qa.q: What was Jatin likely feeling when he had to leave a square half-coloured?
qa.a: He was probably frustrated with himself, because one packet of chips cost him a whole extra week.

qa.q: What would you change first to make Jatin's plan easier at break time?
qa.a: Carrying a snack from home right from week one, as he later did with peanuts, so the canteen smell does not catch him hungry.

qa.q: How might Minakshi-didi see the plan?
qa.a: She seems to support it, since she gave him the tiffin box, and she may be proud to see him stick with it.

grounding: A boy works out how many weeks of saving a football needs, tracks it on a chart and gives up canteen snacks to get there.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: saving for a specific goal [Action]
passage:
"Saurabh, why is there a chart with footballs drawn on the fridge?"
"It's my plan, Preeti. The ball costs four hundred. I get fifty a week. So eight weeks."
"And how many footballs are coloured?"
"Five. Three to go."
"You could just ask Papa."
"I want to buy it myself. Also, look." He pointed to a row of tiny crosses. "Every cross is a day I didn't buy chips at school."
"Sixteen crosses! Don't you miss them?"
"On Tuesdays, yes. Tuesday is samosa-chips day. I eat my banana very slowly."
Preeti laughed. "Can I colour the sixth one next Monday?"
"Only if you don't touch the money tin."
"Deal. And when you get the ball, I'm the goalkeeper."

qa.q: How many footballs on the chart are coloured?
qa.a: Five, with three to go.

qa.q: What does Saurabh eating his banana very slowly on Tuesdays suggest?
qa.a: He still misses the chips and feels tempted, but he is determined to keep to his plan.

qa.q: What other approach could Saurabh have used, and why did he not?
qa.a: He could have asked Papa for the ball, which is quicker, but he wanted the pride of buying it himself.

qa.q: What is it like for Preeti to watch the chart?
qa.a: Preeti seems curious and impressed by the sixteen crosses, and wants to join in by colouring the next football.

grounding: A boy explains his eight-week saving chart for a football and the snacks he skips to reach it.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
passage: On the first Sunday of the month, Nilesh's Dada pressed forty rupees into his palm at the weekly haat in their village. By sunset Nilesh had spent it all: a sheet of shiny cricket stickers, a stick of orange candy, a paper cone of jaggery peanuts and a spinning top he played with once. He stuck the stickers all over his slate and felt rich. The next Sunday, his friend Deepak mentioned that his birthday was on Wednesday. Everyone was bringing something small: a pencil, an eraser, a keyring. Nilesh turned out his pocket and found a peanut shell and one bent sticker. On Wednesday he stood at the back while the others handed over their gifts, his hands pushed deep in his pockets. Deepak smiled at him anyway, but Nilesh walked home quiet.

qa.q: What did Nilesh buy at the haat?
qa.a: A sheet of shiny cricket stickers, a stick of orange candy, a paper cone of jaggery peanuts and a spinning top.

qa.q: What was Nilesh feeling as he stood at the back on Wednesday?
qa.a: He felt ashamed and left out, which shows in his hands pushed deep in his pockets while others gave gifts.

qa.q: What other approach might have left Nilesh something for Wednesday?
qa.a: Keeping part of the forty rupees aside for things that come up, or making Deepak a small handmade gift, would have let him join in.

qa.q: How might Deepak have seen Nilesh at the birthday?
qa.a: Deepak smiled at him anyway, so he seemed to care more about Nilesh being there than about a present.

grounding: A child spends all his pocket money on the first day and has nothing left for a friend's birthday gift the next week.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: spending it all at once on impulse [Pitfall]
passage: Every second Friday, Fatima's mother gave her ten dollars. This time Fatima spent all of it before she even reached home in Toronto: a pack of glitter stickers from the corner shop, a sherbet dip, a bag of gummy worms, and a second pack of stickers because the first had no unicorns. By Sunday the gummy worms were gone and the stickers covered her lunchbox. The next Thursday, Soo-ah handed out small paper invitations to a birthday picnic on Saturday. Fatima's stomach dropped. She checked her jacket pockets, her pencil case and under her bed. Twelve cents. She asked her mother for an early allowance, and her mother gently shook her head. On Saturday Fatima gave Soo-ah a folded card with a drawing, and stood quietly while the other presents were opened.

qa.q: How much money did Fatima find when she searched?
qa.a: Twelve cents.

qa.q: What does Fatima's stomach dropping suggest?
qa.a: She felt a jolt of worry and regret on realising she had nothing left for Soo-ah's present. 😔

qa.q: Which approach would have suited Fatima better when the ten dollars arrived?
qa.a: Waiting a day or two before buying anything, or keeping some back, because invitations and other plans often turn up later in the fortnight.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel about the drawn card?
qa.a: Soo-ah may well like a handmade card; it is Fatima who seems uneasy while the other presents are opened.

grounding: A child spends her whole allowance on impulse and has nothing for a friend's birthday the following week.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: comparing prices at different shops [Thinking]
passage:
Class 5B observation note, Tuesday.
During the stationery check, Nazia told me she had bought her long notebook from the small shop in the lane behind the mosque instead of our school store. I asked why. She said, "Here it's forty-five rupees. There it's thirty-five. Same notebook, same cover. I even checked the page count." She added that the walk takes about six minutes and she passes that lane anyway with her brother. "So ten rupees for six minutes. I'm putting it toward crayons." She sounded quite pleased with herself. I asked the class whether anyone else had noticed prices changing from shop to shop, and three children started comparing at once. Next week I will run a short maths activity on prices using real shop lists.
Joseph, class teacher

qa.q: How much did the notebook cost at the lane shop?
qa.a: Thirty-five rupees.

qa.q: How did Nazia seem to feel about what she had worked out?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and proud that a six-minute walk saved her ten rupees for crayons.

qa.q: What else could Nazia compare besides the price, and why?
qa.a: Whether the paper and page count really match, which she checked, and whether the walk is safe; going with her brother matters as much as the saving.

qa.q: How did the classmates respond when Joseph raised Nazia's idea?
qa.a: Three children started comparing prices at once, so Nazia's thinking sparked interest across the class.

grounding: A teacher's note records a girl explaining why buying a notebook at a cheaper lane shop is worth a short walk.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: comparing prices at different shops [Thinking]
passage:
Thursday night
Dear diary, today I found out something. The school store sells the brown-cover notebook for sixty rupees. After school Nandini and I walked down the lane to buy pencils at the corner shop, and there it was, the SAME notebook for fifty! I kept both prices in my head all the way home. Ten rupees is not much, I thought, but I need four notebooks this term. Four times ten is forty. Forty rupees could be the glitter pens I keep looking at. The lane is only a little further, and Nandini goes that way anyway. Tomorrow I'll tell Amma I want to buy them there. Walking a bit more isn't hard. Being clever with money feels nice!
Rekha

qa.q: How many notebooks does Rekha need this term?
qa.a: Four notebooks.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling after working out the forty rupees?
qa.a: Rekha felt excited and a little proud, writing that being clever with money feels nice.

qa.q: What else could Rekha check before buying all four notebooks at the lane shop?
qa.a: Rekha could ask Amma whether walking the lane is fine and whether the shop usually has the notebook, so the plan works every time.

qa.q: How might Amma see Rekha's idea?
qa.a: Amma may be pleased that Rekha worked out the saving alone, though Amma might want to know Rekha walks with Nandini.

grounding: A diary entry shows a child comparing a notebook's price at two shops and deciding the short walk frees money for something else.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: waiting a few days before buying [Thinking]
passage: On Thursday evening, in the toy corner of the Rajouri market, Uday could not stop looking at a remote-control jeep with flashing wheels. It would take almost all his birthday money. "Mumma, please, today?" His mother, Bhavna, said, "Let's both wait three days. If you still want it on Sunday, we'll come back." Uday nodded, but he sulked in the auto all the way home. On Friday he drew the jeep in his notebook. On Saturday he mentioned it once. On Sunday morning a friend showed him a new pack of cricket cards, and Uday spent an hour sorting his own. When Bhavna asked about the jeep, he thought for a while. "It's nice... but the wheels will only flash for a week. The cards I'll keep trading all year. I'll keep the money for those."

qa.q: What did Uday want to buy at the market?
qa.a: A remote-control jeep with flashing wheels.

qa.q: How had Uday's feelings changed by Sunday?
qa.a: His excitement had faded; he felt calm and thoughtful enough to decide the cards would give him longer-lasting fun.

qa.q: Which other approach might suit Uday next time, and why?
qa.a: He could put the jeep and the cards side by side and ask which he would still enjoy in a month, since that shows lasting value before he spends.

qa.q: How might Bhavna see the waiting plan?
qa.a: She is probably relieved that Uday chose for himself instead of being refused, so there was no fight at the shop.

grounding: A boy agrees to wait three days before buying a toy and finds his wish has faded in favour of cricket cards.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: waiting a few days before buying [Thinking]
passage:
"Mummy, it's day three," Kunal announced at breakfast.
Jyoti looked up from her tea. "Day three of what?"
"The battle top. You said wait three days, then decide."
"I did. So? Still want it?"
Kunal chewed his paratha slowly. "On day one I wanted it so much my stomach hurt. Yesterday I only thought about it at night. Today..." He shrugged. "Rohit's top broke in one week. And the new cricket cards have come to the shop."
"So which is it?"
"The top is fun for five minutes. The cards I can swap with the whole building. I think I'll keep the money for cards."
"You're sure? I won't say I told you so."
Kunal grinned. "You just did, Mummy."

qa.q: What did Kunal want before the three days of waiting?
qa.a: The battle top.

qa.q: How did Kunal's feelings about the top change over the three days?
qa.a: On day one he wanted it so badly his stomach hurt; by day three the excitement had faded and he felt calm enough to choose the cards.

qa.q: What else could Kunal have done to test his wish?
qa.a: He could have tried a friend's top for an afternoon, since playing with something often shows whether the wanting will last.

qa.q: What is it like for Jyoti to hear Kunal's decision?
qa.a: Jyoti seems amused and pleased, teasing that she won't say she told him so. 😊

grounding: A boy waits three days before buying a toy and decides to keep the money for cricket cards instead.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: copying what a friend buys [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Gargi, Joseph's older sister, and I saw the whole pen business. Last month Tarak came to school with a shiny blue pen with a gold clip, the kind where you can see the ink. By Friday half of Joseph's class had asked to hold it. On Saturday Joseph emptied his piggy bank, three hundred rupees, and bought the same pen at the stationery shop. He wrote his name ten times that evening. By Wednesday he was back to his old chewed pencil for homework. The new pen stayed in his bag. When I asked, he said, "It's heavy and it smudges when I write fast." Then, quieter: "I wanted the geometry set with the protractor." I don't know if he was sad about the money or about Tarak. He didn't say.

qa.q: How much did Joseph pay for the pen?
qa.a: Three hundred rupees, the whole of his piggy bank.

qa.q: What might Joseph have been feeling when he said he wanted the geometry set?
qa.a: He seemed disappointed and regretful, speaking more quietly about what he had really wanted.

qa.q: What else could Joseph have tried before spending his savings?
qa.a: He could have borrowed Tarak's pen for a day of homework, or waited a week, to see whether he really liked it.

qa.q: How does Gargi read Joseph's mood?
qa.a: Gargi notices the unused pen and the quiet voice but admits not knowing whether Joseph was sad about the money or about Tarak.

grounding: An older sibling watches a boy spend his savings on the same pen as a classmate and then regret not choosing his own thing.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: copying what a friend buys [Pitfall]
passage:
Monday: Chandrika uncapped a silver fountain pen in class and everyone around her said "ooh". Kunal watched her write the date in curly letters. At lunch he asked how much it cost. "Two hundred and fifty," she said. He had exactly that saved for a box of twenty-four sketch pens.
Wednesday: Kunal bought the silver pen. At first he held it the way Chandrika did. By the second page his fingers were blue and the ink had blotted his answer twice.
The next Monday: the fountain pen lay in his pencil box, dry. In art class Kunal borrowed a sketch pen from the boy beside him and coloured a sunset, pressing too hard. "I should've got my own thing," he muttered to no one.

qa.q: How much did the silver pen cost?
qa.a: Two hundred and fifty, exactly what Kunal had saved for sketch pens.

qa.q: What does Kunal pressing too hard while colouring suggest?
qa.a: He felt frustrated and regretful about spending his savings on a pen he did not enjoy instead of the sketch pens he wanted.

qa.q: What would you change first in Kunal's plan?
qa.a: Before buying, he could ask himself what he would actually use the pen for; his own plan, the sketch pens, fitted what he loves doing.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see Kunal buying the same pen?
qa.a: She may hardly notice, or feel a little flattered; she has no idea it cost Kunal his sketch-pen savings.

grounding: Over a week, a boy copies a classmate's expensive pen, finds it does not suit him and wishes he had bought what he wanted.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: keeping a small notebook of spending [Action]
passage: On the first of March in Valencia, Valentina's grandmother gave her a small green notebook. "Write down every coin you spend, all month." Valentina did: 1.20 for a pastry at the bakery, 0.80 for gum, 1.50 for crisps after swimming. On the thirty-first she sat with her best friend Ines and added it all up in pencil. Snacks: eighteen euros. Everything else: four. She stared at the page. She was saving for roller skates and had been stuck at thirty euros for weeks. In April she packed an apple and a bag of almonds for swimming days, and the bakery became a Saturday thing. By mid-May the skates were in a box under her bed, three weeks sooner than she had guessed.

qa.q: How much had Valentina spent on snacks in March?
qa.a: Eighteen euros.

qa.q: What does Valentina staring at the page suggest?
qa.a: She felt surprised, even a little shocked, that snacks had taken most of her money.

qa.q: What else could help Valentina keep the notebook useful?
qa.a: She could look over it with her grandmother each week rather than once a month, since spotting a pattern early lets her change sooner.

qa.q: How might Ines see the notebook plan?
qa.a: Ines helped add it up, so Ines saw the eighteen euros too and might be curious to try tracking spending as well.

grounding: A girl records every coin she spends for a month, sees how much goes on snacks and reaches her saving goal sooner by bringing food from home.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: keeping a small notebook of spending [Action]
passage: Every Saturday at the Hillcrest hostel, the matron handed out tuck money from a locked box. For all of October, Trisha wrote each rupee in a thin notebook: 10 for chikki, 15 for juice, 20 for a samosa after football. On the last Sunday she added it up in the common room. Out of four hundred rupees, two hundred and sixty had gone on snacks. "That's more than half," said Varun, her twin, peering over. Trisha wanted a three-hundred-rupee torch for the class camping trip. In November she asked the mess in-charge if she could carry fruit from breakfast, and kept a banana or a guava in her kit bag for after football. By the third week of November, the torch money was ready.

qa.q: How much of the four hundred rupees went on snacks?
qa.a: Two hundred and sixty rupees.

qa.q: What might Trisha have felt when Varun said it was more than half?
qa.a: She was probably surprised and a bit embarrassed, but it also seemed to make her determined to change.

qa.q: Which other approach could help Trisha if the fruit runs out?
qa.a: She could check the notebook every week instead of once a month, so she notices extra snack spending sooner.

qa.q: How does Varun see the notebook?
qa.a: Varun is curious and peers over; the plain total makes the pattern obvious even to someone else. 🤔

grounding: A hostel girl logs every rupee for a month, sees how much goes on snacks and switches to fruit to reach her saving goal.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: goal too big for the time available [Revision]
passage: In Class 6 maths, Mrs Kulkarni wrote a problem on the board: "You save twenty rupees a week. How long to buy a cycle costing two thousand rupees?" Santosh worked it out quickly, and his face fell. A hundred weeks. Almost two years. That was his cycle, the red one in the shop near the bus depot. At break he sat on the school steps and redrew his plan: a cricket bat for six hundred first. Thirty weeks, still long but possible. Then another idea. After the last bell, his uncle, Darshan-mama, was waiting at the school gate as usual. "Mama, can I help with chores at your house on Sundays? Watering, sweeping the verandah? To earn a bit extra?" Darshan-mama smiled and said they would ask Santosh's mother together that evening.

qa.q: How many weeks would the cycle take at twenty rupees a week?
qa.a: A hundred weeks, almost two years.

qa.q: What did Santosh's falling face show?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and discouraged on realising the cycle was nearly two years away.

qa.q: What else could Santosh do if the chores bring in only a little?
qa.a: He could keep the bat as his first goal and talk with his family about whether the cycle might be a shared gift later on.

qa.q: How might Darshan-mama see Santosh's request?
qa.a: He seems pleased, smiling, and wants to ask Santosh's mother together, respecting both the effort and the family's say.

grounding: A boy sees his savings target is too far off, switches to a cheaper goal and asks his uncle about earning extra through chores.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: goal too big for the time available [Revision]
passage: I'm Imran, and Yusuf and I share a bench in class. For weeks he talked only about the geared cycle in the window of the cycle shop: two thousand rupees. Every Friday he counted his coins at lunch. Last Friday he stopped halfway, scribbled on the back of his notebook and went very quiet. I peeked: "25 a week... 80 weeks." Then he crossed out CYCLE and wrote "football boots, 500". After school I was with him when his Chacha came to pick him up. Yusuf asked straight out, "Chacha, can I wash your scooter on Sundays and help at the stall? For some extra money?" His Chacha laughed and said yes, starting this Sunday. Yusuf walked home faster than usual. I think he was happy. Or relieved.

qa.q: What did Yusuf write after crossing out CYCLE?
qa.a: "Football boots, 500".

qa.q: Why did Yusuf go very quiet last Friday?
qa.a: He had just worked out that the cycle would take eighty weeks, and he seemed discouraged before he changed his plan.

qa.q: Which approach would you suggest to Yusuf if the chores money stays small?
qa.a: Keep the boots as the next goal and look at the cycle again later, perhaps with his family, rather than dropping the idea altogether.

qa.q: How does Imran read Yusuf's mood on the way home?
qa.a: Imran sees Yusuf walking faster and guesses happy or relieved, without being sure which.

grounding: A classmate watches a boy realise his cycle goal would take too long, switch to boots and ask his uncle for chores.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: choosing between two wants using needs versus wants [Thinking]
passage: Maria stood outside the stationery shop in Andheri with three hundred rupees from her aunt folded in her fist. Two things pulled at her: the geometry box her maths teacher wanted by Monday, and a handheld puzzle game glowing in the next window. Her friend Sunaina said, "Get the game. You can borrow my compass." Maria took out a pencil and made two columns on an old receipt: NEED and WANT. Under NEED: "Geometry box. Monday. Whole class will have one." Under WANT: "Game. Fun, but no deadline." She looked at the words for a while. "If I borrow yours every day, you'll get fed up. And the game will still be here next month." She bought the box for a hundred and forty and zipped the rest into her pencil pouch for the game.

qa.q: What did Maria write as the two column headings?
qa.a: NEED and WANT.

qa.q: What might Maria have been feeling as she looked at the words for a while?
qa.a: She felt torn, pulled by the game, but she worried that borrowing Sunaina's compass every day would wear on the friendship.

qa.q: What else could have helped Maria decide?
qa.a: She could have asked the aunt who gave her the money, since talking it over with an adult can make the choice feel clearer.

subtopic: Deciding what to do with pocket money
subtype: Approach: choosing between two wants using needs versus wants [Thinking]
passage:
"Akka, help me. I have five hundred from Pongal. I want the snakes-and-ladders set with the dice tower. But my bag strap tore again today."
Manjula didn't look up from her book. "Make two lists. Need. Want."
"Fine." Leela scribbled. "Need: bag, because I can't carry books with one strap. Want: the game, because it's fun."
"And which one do you use every day?"
"The bag. Every single day." Leela sighed. "The game is only for holidays."
"So?"
"So the bag first." She tapped the paper. "The bag is three-fifty. Then I have one-fifty left. The game is four hundred, so I save two-fifty more."
Manjula finally smiled. "You worked that out yourself, not me."

qa.q: How much does the game cost?
qa.a: Four hundred.

qa.q: How did Leela feel on seeing that the bag is needed every day?
qa.a: She sighed, a little disappointed to put the game second, but seemed settled once she had a plan for it.

qa.q: What else could Leela try to reach the game sooner?
qa.a: She could look for a simpler version of the game, or play a friend's copy while she saves, so the wait feels shorter.

qa.q: How does Manjula see Leela's reasoning?
qa.a: Manjula seems proud of her, pointing out that Leela worked it out herself.

grounding: A girl sorts a bag and a board game into needs and wants, chooses the bag first and plans to save for the game.
